module.title: A/B Testing for Product Managers
module.subtitle: 100+ EXERCISES / 40 HOURS OF PRACTICE
module.description: You don't need to be a statistician to run good experiments — you need the principles. Read results, avoid the traps, decide ship/no-ship. Case: Calmly meditation app.

lesson.title: Experiments: Ship, Kill, or Keep Running?
lesson.note: Uses an ab-result widget (a small results table: variant, users, metric, uplift, p-value/CI, power). Fixture-driven from each tool block's config. Same grading model. The learning goal is interpretation and decision-making, not hand computation.

blocks.markdown: I run experimentation at **Calmly**. Experiments are the only way to know if a change *caused* an improvement. You don't need heavy stats — you need to read results correctly and not get fooled. Let's go.
We want a bigger 'Start free trial' button. Before we build anything — what makes a good **hypothesis** for this test?

options.label: 'A larger CTA will increase trial-start rate, because it's easier to notice' — a change, an expected metric move, and a reason
'Let's make the button bigger and see what happens'
'The button should be blue'

blocks.markdown: A hypothesis names the change, the **primary metric** it should move, and a rationale. 'See what happens' has no falsifiable prediction — you'll rationalize any result after the fact.
Here's the first readout. Primary metric = trial-start rate. Is this a ship?

options.label: Ship — +12% uplift, p=0.01, CI excludes 0, and the test was powered
Don't ship — 5.6% vs 5.0% is basically the same
Run it 3 more months to be sure

blocks.markdown: Clean win: statistically significant (p=0.01), the confidence interval is entirely positive (+3% to +21%), and the test was adequately powered. When all three line up, ship.
Next readout. Same button, different week. Ship?

options.label: Not yet — p=0.21 and the CI includes 0; the sample is too small (underpowered)
Ship — +28% is even bigger than last time!
Ship the control, it's safer

blocks.markdown: A big point-estimate on a tiny sample is a mirage. p=0.21 means this could easily be noise, and the CI spans negative to +62% — you genuinely don't know the sign. Underpowered tests produce large, unstable effects. Collect more data before deciding.
Impatient stakeholder: 'It hit p<0.05 on day 2! Let's stop the test and ship.' Why is stopping the moment you see significance a problem?

options.label: Peeking / early stopping inflates false positives — significance can appear by chance then vanish; decide at the pre-set sample size
No problem — p<0.05 is p<0.05 whenever it happens
Day 2 is unlucky, wait for day 3 then stop

blocks.markdown: 'Peeking' and stopping at the first significant blip massively inflates the false-positive rate. Fix the sample size (or use a sequential-testing method designed for it) up front, and read the result at the end.
This variant increased trial-starts (+10%, significant) but 30-day **paid retention dropped** 8%. What does this tell you about metric choice?

options.label: The change attracted lower-intent trials — guardrail metrics matter; a primary win with a retention loss may be net-negative
Ship — the primary metric won, retention is irrelevant
Retention always drops, ignore it

blocks.markdown: Optimizing one metric can harm another. Always define **guardrail metrics** (retention, revenue, complaints). A cheaper trigger that pulls in users who churn fast can lose money despite a shiny top-line win.
Someone ran ONE test but measured 20 different metrics, and reports 'we found a significant effect on scroll-depth (p=0.04)!' Why be skeptical?

options.label: Multiple comparisons — test 20 metrics at p<0.05 and ~1 will look significant by pure chance; wasn't the pre-declared primary metric
Scroll-depth is a great primary metric
p=0.04 is always trustworthy

blocks.markdown: With 20 metrics at 5%, you expect ~1 false positive by chance. Cherry-picking the one that 'worked' is p-hacking. Declare a single primary metric before the test; treat everything else as exploratory.
A test comes back **flat** — no significant difference, and it was well-powered. The team is deflated. What's the right framing?

options.label: A trustworthy null result is valuable — it saved us shipping something that doesn't help; keep control and move on
Ship the variant anyway, we built it
Keep running until it turns significant

blocks.markdown: Most experiments don't win — that's normal and useful. A powered null tells you not to invest further. Shipping anyway ('we built it' — the sunk-cost trap) or running until noise crosses the line both defeat the purpose.
Final: results are strong, but you notice **80% of traffic went to Variant and 20% to Control** (misconfigured split), and Variant skews to iOS users. Trust it?

options.label: No — a broken split / sample-ratio mismatch suggests biased assignment; re-run with a correct 50/50 randomization
Yes — more users in Variant means more confidence
Yes — iOS users are the important ones

blocks.markdown: A **sample-ratio mismatch** (getting 80/20 when you expected 50/50) means randomization is broken — the groups aren't comparable, so any 'result' is confounded (here, by platform). Fix the assignment and re-run; don't trust a compromised experiment.

Strong work. You can write a real hypothesis, read significance + confidence intervals + power together, resist peeking and p-hacking, respect guardrails, value null results, and catch a broken experiment. That's experiment literacy — the thing that lets a PM out-argue anyone with data.
